## Introduction

The `backyardWTC` package provides an interactive way to explore runner performance at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championships.

It is designed for backyard ultra spectators, running enthusiasts and performance analysts interested in comparing results across nations and competition classes.

This vignette explains how to install the package, launch the Shiny application, explore its outputs and interpret the results.

## Installation

The development version of `backyardWTC` can be installed from GitHub.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")

remotes::install_github(
  "ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-jban0020"
)
```

Once installed, load the package:

```{r}
library(backyardWTC)
```

## Launching the Shiny application

The main feature of the package is an interactive Shiny dashboard.

Launch it using:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
backyardWTC::run_wtc_app()
```

The dashboard opens in a browser and allows users to explore performance among stopped runners.

## Exploring the dashboard

The application provides several controls for comparing runner performance.

### Choosing a comparison

Use the **Compare performance by** menu to switch between:

- Nation: compare runners representing different countries.
- Competition class: compare runners across the four recorded classes.

### Applying filters

The sidebar allows users to:

- Select one or more nations, or leave the selection blank to include all nations.
- Select which competition classes to include.
- Set the minimum number of completed yards.
- Choose mean or median yards as the performance measure.
- Adjust the number of nations shown in the chart.

The chart and summary table update automatically when these settings change.

### Example exploration

Suppose you want to compare nations with runners who completed at least 50 yards.

1. Select **Nation** as the comparison.
2. Set **Minimum completed yards** to 50.
3. Keep all competition classes selected.
4. Select **Median yards** as the performance measure.
5. Examine the resulting chart and summary table.

This allows you to compare performance among runners who reached the selected threshold.

## Interpreting the outputs

### Performance chart

The bar chart displays either the mean or median completed yards for each nation or competition class.

The **median** represents the middle yard count within a group, while the **mean** represents the arithmetic average.

Each bar is labelled with the number of runners contributing to that group's summary.

When comparing nations, the chart displays the highest-ranked nations according to the selected performance measure.

### Summary table

The table provides additional statistics for every group matching the selected filters.

These include:

- **Runners:** Number of stopped runners in the group.
- **Mean yards:** Average completed yards.
- **Median yards:** Middle completed yard count.
- **Maximum yards:** Highest completed yard count.
- **Total yards:** Combined completed yards across runners.

The table is useful for comparing performance while considering differences in group sizes.

A high group median does not necessarily indicate that the group had the greatest total number of completed yards.

## Working with the data directly

The package also includes the `wtc_stopped` dataset.

```{r}
head(
  wtc_stopped[
    , c("runner", "nation", "class", "yards")
  ]
)
```

The `summarise_stopped_runners()` function allows users to generate summaries without opening the dashboard.

For example, summarise performance by competition class:

```{r}
summarise_stopped_runners(
  group = "class"
)
```

Alternatively, compare nations after restricting the data to runners completing at least 50 yards:

```{r}
head(
  summarise_stopped_runners(
    group = "nation",
    min_yards = 50
  )
)
```

The function returns the same core summary measures used by the Shiny application.

## Important limitations

The dataset contains 925 stopped-runner records from a snapshot taken after yard 124 of the 2026 championships.

It does not represent the complete championship roster or official team standings.

Consequently, the results describe performance among runners recorded as stopped in this snapshot, rather than the final performance of every championship participant.

Comparisons involving groups with relatively few runners should also be interpreted cautiously.

The original data was obtained from the [WTC 2026 Live Dashboard](https://wtc2026.bigsbackyardultra.com/#race).

## Conclusion

The `backyardWTC` package provides two ways to explore runner performance: an interactive Shiny application and an R summary function.

Together, these tools allow users to compare nations and competition classes, investigate different performance measures and explore the championship data while remaining aware of its limitations.
